title: Centrifuge Levee Failure Test
description: ERDC researchers at the Centrifuge Research Complex have been working closely with Virginia Tech to validate their mathematical models by physically modelling a levee culvert failure. Simultaneously, the team is testing a variety of detection techniques to serve as early warning systems for levee managers.
unit_name: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Engineer Research and Development Center

transcript.text: So today , we were looking at internal
erosion into a levee . There's a number
of different failure modes that occur
during internal erosion . And we chose
to model internal erosion into a
culvert . During that process , there
is a a culvert defect , maybe it's a
misaligned joint or a crush section or
some sort of erosion that occurred .
And one is able to start seeping into
that cult during its normal seepage
path . And when it does that ,
sometimes it takes some of the fine
grains of the soil with it . And so the
erosion channel eventually can
propagate and create total failure of
the levee . Understanding this process
is kind of multi fold . This particular
project , we really wanted to know what
kind of early warning signs might there
be so that we can fix a problem before
it gets too extreme . And two , we
wanted to see can instruments or
monitoring help us identify odd
changes or things that we wouldn't
expect . We had to make a false bottom
for it to build the levee on top of .
So the water could come off the other
end , we had to make a soul catch and a
V weir to measure outflow , we had
inflow and outflow readings on it . We
had PPT pore pressure sensor
transducers . So we've had a bunch of
different sensors on it . I think we
finally got it down to an art now . So
what started out as a two week deal for
us to build a levy ? We can do it in
two days . Now , we saw in test two
that a little bit before it reached the
surface , we could see a bit of a
seepage path through the IR camera ,
but it still would have been a little
too late in the real world . So I think
it's a promising technique , but
there's definitely more research that
needs to be done before it can be used
in the field . It's always a team
effort . Our technicians are amazing

reality ? And we'll work with our

have these parts and this might work
well , what do you guys think ? When

you would never think I want a

that you've learned go into centrifuge

your test to be a success . But
sometimes you just don't know if some
of the things you put on the model are
going to work . Sometimes you don't
know if a certain motor or a certain

never really know what's going to
happen until you spin it up . It can
definitely be a little tense and
usually it's because we all care so

from this and what problems can we

Virginia Tech . So they are doing MPM
modeling , which is the material point
method and they're able to model large
deformations using numerical modeling .
In numerical modeling . It's much
easier to run different simulations ,
try different sizes , that sort of
thing , but you know , it's not always
validated . So in the centrifuge , we
can , we can run a few tests and really
help validate their model and using the
two of them together can really help
tell a story and shape our
understanding .
